Which label format does this follow?

The bar coded cargo label in IATA Resolution 606: airline name, air waybill number, destination and a Code 128 primary barcode as mandatory items, plus the optional items such as origin, transfer points, pieces, weights and house waybill details.
Can it read my air waybill file?

Yes. Choose or drop a PDF, JPG or PNG of the air waybill and the tool fills in the airline, AWB number, origin, destination, total pieces and weight. Optional details such as transfer points and handling information are left blank for you to add if you want them. PDFs from airline and e-AWB systems read best. Scans and photos work too if they are sharp and straight. Fields in green passed our checks, fields in amber need a look. The file is read on your own device and never uploaded.
What printer and label size should I use?

A 4×6 inch (or 10×15 cm) direct thermal label printer gives the best barcodes. You can also print on A4 paper, four labels per page, and stick them on with clear tape. Always print at 100% size, without fit-to-page scaling.
Do I need one label per piece?

Yes. Each piece carries its own label, and the piece number is part of the barcode, so every label in a shipment is different. You can print a range, for example pieces 11 to 20, if you are labelling in batches.
What does the check digit warning mean?

The last digit of an 8-digit air waybill serial is normally the first seven digits divided by 7, taking the remainder. If it does not match, the number may have been mistyped. Check it against your air waybill.
Can I use these for dangerous goods?
You can use them as the air waybill label, but dangerous goods and lithium batteries also need their own hazard labels and marks. You can download those free from our dangerous goods labels page.
